title: Chapter 17: Scope and Good Function Design
video_title: Python Chapter 17: Scope and Good Function Design
summary: Asha's oldest function adds tax, prints a line and changes a global week total, all at once. Follow her as she learns local and global scope, fixes a NameError and an UnboundLocalError, and uses default and keyword arguments. Then watch her split the function with an AI assistant at all six stages, checking every change against her saved output.

scenes.title: Introduction
scenes.direction: Open on Asha's oldest function doing three jobs, in her words. Then the title with the AI tease, then the redesigned day report as the mission, with no output yet.

visual.heading: One function, three jobs
visual.label: The problem
body: Asha's oldest function at the Corner Cafe closes the day.
visual.pre:
def close_day(day, prices):
      global week_total             <- changes something outside
      total = 0
      for price in prices:
          total += round(price * 1.1, 2)    <- calculates
      total = round(total, 2)
      print(...)                    <- prints
      week_total = ...              <- and updates the week

segments.say: At the Corner Cafe, Asha's oldest function closes the day. It adds the tax, prints a line, and changes a week total, all at once.
When one part goes wrong, she has to read all of it. And Chapter 16 ended with a question: day total has a variable called total inside it. Can the rest of the program see it?

scenes.title: The idea: where a variable lives
scenes.direction: Teach scope with the table and the diagram, then the kitchen analogy and where it stops working, then the rule. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Two scopes
visual.label: The idea
rows: Inside a function: an assignment or a parameter
Only inside that function, while it runs
At the top level of the file
Everywhere in the file; functions can read it

segments.say: The scope of a variable is the part of the program where its name can be used. A local variable is created inside a function. It exists only while that function runs.
A global variable is created at the top level of the file. Every function can read it.

visual.heading: The menu board and the whiteboard
visual.label: The idea
body: Inside a function, Python looks for a local name first, then a global one.
visual.pre:
tax_rate = 1.1                 <- global: the menu board

  def day_total(prices):
      total = 0                  <- local: the kitchen whiteboard
      ...                        <- can read tax_rate

  print(total)                   <- NameError: total is gone

segments.say: Think of the cafe. The menu board on the wall is global: everyone can read it, even the cook. The kitchen whiteboard is local: its notes are wiped when the job is done.

Where it stops working: suppose the cook writes a note with the same name as something on the menu board. Python treats that name as a kitchen note for the whole function, even on the lines before the note.

visual.heading: The design rule
visual.label: The idea
items: Pass values in as parameters. Return results out.
A **pure function** uses only its parameters and returns its result. It prints nothing and changes nothing outside.
A pure function gives the same result for the same arguments, so one line can test it.

segments.say: So good functions follow one rule: pass values in as parameters, and return results out.
A function that uses only its parameters and returns its result, without printing or changing anything outside, is called a pure function. One line can test it.

visual.question: A variable is created inside a function. Where can you use it?
options: Only inside that function, while it runs
visual.explain: It is local: it exists only while the function runs.

segments.say: Quick check. A variable is created inside a function. Where can you use it?

after.say: C. Only inside that function, while it runs. It is local.

items: Local: inside a function, while it runs.
Global: the top level of the file.
Pass values in, return results out.

segments.say: Take a breather. Next, Asha tests these rules with real code.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: Local and global
scenes.direction: Ask what lines 8 and 9 of ex01 print, then what lines 7 and 9 of ex02 print.

visual.heading: Step 1: A local variable
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 1. Inside day total, line 3 creates a variable called total. That makes it local.
Line 8 calls the function and prints what it returns. Line 9 tries to print total itself.

after.say: Line 8 prints 7.5, the returned value.
Line 9 stops with a Name Error. Total existed only while the function ran. To use a result outside, return it and store it.

visual.heading: Step 2: A function reads a global
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 2. Line 2 creates tax rate at the top level, so it is global. With tax reads it on line 5.
Line 7 calls with tax. Line 8 changes tax rate to 1.2. And line 9 makes exactly the same call again.

after.say: 3.85, then 4.2. The same call gives two results, because the function reads tax rate at the moment it runs.
Nothing in the call shows that hidden link to line 8. That is why good functions take what they need as parameters.

scenes.title: Step 3: Changing a global inside a function
scenes.direction: Teach the assignment rule, ask where Python stops, reveal the UnboundLocalError, then the pass-in, return-out fix.

visual.heading: Step 3: Counting sales with a global

segments.say: Step 3. Asha counts sales with a global variable, sales count, on line 2.
Line 5 assigns to sales count inside the function. Remember the rule: an assignment makes the name local for the whole function.

ask.question: Where does Python stop, and why?

after.say: On line 5. The right side reads the local sales count before it has a value. Python calls this an Unbound Local Error.
The traceback shows the call on line 7, then the failing line 5 inside the function.
Python has a keyword, global, that allows the change. But it brings back the hidden link from step 2. There is a better fix.

visual.heading: The fix: pass it in, return it out

segments.say: Add sale now takes the count as a parameter, and returns the count plus 1.
Lines 6 and 7 store each returned value. Two sales, so line 8 prints 2.

scenes.title: Steps 4 and 5: Default and keyword arguments
scenes.direction: Teach defaults and ask about lines 5 and 7. Teach keyword arguments and their order rule, ask about line 7. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 4: A default argument
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 4. A default argument is a value a parameter gets when the call leaves it out. Here, rate equals 1.1 in the def line.
Parameters with a default must come after the parameters without one. Line 6 passes a rate of 1.2. Lines 5 and 7 leave the rate out.

after.say: 3.85 and 4.4. Both calls leave out the rate, so it is 1.1.
Line 6 prints 4.2 with its own rate. Now nothing is hidden: the rate is a parameter.
One more fact about defaults: Python creates a default value once, when the def line runs, not at each call. For a number, that makes no difference. Remember it for later.

visual.heading: Step 5: Keyword arguments
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 5. A keyword argument names the parameter in the call. On line 7, q t y equals 2 says at once what the 2 means.
A positional argument is matched by its position: first to first. Keyword arguments can come in any order, but after any positional ones. Line 8 names both, in a new order.

after.say: 1 x Scone, 2.75. Q t y keeps its default, 1, and the names put each value in the right place.
Line 6 uses the default too, and line 7 gives 2 cakes for 8.00.

visual.question: `def order_line(item, price, qty=1):` Which call is NOT allowed?
visual.explain: After a keyword argument, every argument needs a name.

segments.say: Quick check. Which of these calls is not allowed?

after.say: A. A positional argument cannot come after a keyword argument.

items: Change a value by returning it.
Defaults go last in the `def` line.
Keywords go last in the call.

segments.say: Breather. Relax for a moment. Next, the most important design rule: one job per function.

scenes.title: Step 6: One job per function
scenes.direction: Show a calculation function and a text function, and why line 13 can test the first one.

visual.heading: Step 6: One job each

segments.say: Step 6. Day total has one job: it calculates and returns.
Total line has one job: it builds the text. Neither function prints.
Only the main code prints. And line 13 tests day total with one comparison: True. A function that only prints could never be tested like that.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the day report, redesigned
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Walk the three functions, the default rate and the two local totals, ask what line 19 prints, reveal, then hand over to the AI feature.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the redesigned day report
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Back to the mission. With tax takes the rate as a default argument, instead of a fixed number.
Day total and report line take the rate too, and pass it on to the next function.
Report line has its own local variable called total, on line 15. Day total has one too. The two never meet: each lives only inside its own function.
Line 19 reports Friday, a day with a higher tax, using a keyword argument for the rate.

after.say: Friday, 2 sales, 9.30. The rate of 1.2 travels from the call into every function.
Line 18 uses the default rate, and line 20 tests a total in one line: True. Mission complete!

visual.heading: Write: your own function first

messages.text: Before any split, I wrote the calculation myself as a pure function. Do not change it. Predict exactly what the last two lines print.
Correct. I also ran the original program and saved its output. This is my target:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Before asking for a split, Asha writes the calculation herself, as a pure day total. The AI predicts 11.28 and 8.53, and her run agrees.
Then she runs the original program and saves its real output. That is her target for every change.

visual.heading: Generate: a split with rules

messages.text: Split close_day into small functions with one job each. Use no global variables. Return results instead of printing them. The output must stay exactly the same.
Here is the split: `day_total()` and `report_line()`, and no globals. The output stays exactly the same.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for a split with clear rules: no global variables, return instead of print, and exactly the same output.
The AI writes day total and report line, and promises the same output. Its day total matches the one Asha wrote herself.

visual.heading: The AI's split, before Asha runs it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Here is the whole split. Look at line 10, inside report line. Then look at lines 14 and 15.

ask.question: The AI says the output is exactly the same. Is it right?

after.say: No. Two extra lines say None. Report line prints instead of returning, so it returns None.
Lines 14 and 15 print that None too. Asha's saved target caught it at once. The AI broke its own rule, and it sounded sure.

visual.heading: Test: cases with expected lines

messages.text: Your report_line prints instead of returning, so my program printed None twice. Fix it. Then give me three test cases with the exact expected line: a normal day, an empty day and a day with one sale.

Change `print(` to `return` on line 10.
Test cases: Monday `[3.5, 4.0, 2.75]` gives `Monday   3 sales  11.28`. Sunday `[]` gives `Sunday   0 sales   0.00`. Friday `[2.0]` gives `Friday   1 sales   2.20`.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha tells the AI what happened. She asks for the fix, and for three test cases with the exact expected line: a normal day, an empty day, and one sale.
The AI changes print to return on line 10, and lists the three cases. Asha checks Monday against her target, and counts the spaces in the other two.

visual.heading: The three cases, on the AI's first version

segments.say: First, she runs the three cases on the AI's first version. Every case fails, because report line still prints and returns None.

visual.heading: The three cases, on the fixed split

segments.say: Lines 12 to 14 hold the three cases: a day, its prices, and the expected line. The loop on line 15 runs each one through report line.
Line 17 prints pass or FAIL, with the if else from Chapter 14. All three pass, including the empty day.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I added a function for the week total, and got this error. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha moves the week total into its own function, and Python stops. She pastes the code and the full error, and asks for the cause first.

visual.heading: Debug: a fix that keeps the rules

messages.text: I added a function for the week total, and got this error. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

Line 5 assigns to `week_total`, so Python treats it as local in `add_to_week()`. Then it reads that local name before it has a value.
The fix: add `global week_total` as the first line of the function.
My plan says no global variables. Show a fix that passes the week total in and returns the new total.

segments.say: The AI explains the cause well: line 5 assigns to week total, so it is local, and it is read before it has a value. But its fix is to add the global keyword.
That breaks Asha's own plan: no global variables. So she asks for a fix that passes the week total in, and returns the new one.

visual.heading: The final split, checked again

segments.say: Add to week now takes the week total in, and returns the new one. Lines 19 and 20 add Monday and Tuesday.
Asha runs everything again. The output matches her target exactly, week total 19.81, and all three cases pass.

visual.heading: Improve: one suggestion

messages.text: My split passes every test. Suggest one improvement, with one reason. Keep the output the same.
Add `record_sale(price, sales=[])`. With a default empty list, you can record a day's sales one by one without making a list first. Everything else stays the same.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one improvement that keeps the output the same.
The AI suggests a record sale function with a default empty list, so she can record sales one by one.

visual.heading: Testing the suggestion with two days
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Asha tests it with two separate days. Lines 6 and 7 record two Monday sales. Line 8 records one Tuesday sale, and leaves out the list.

after.say: No. Both lists hold all three sales. Python creates a default value once, when the def line runs, not at each call.
Remember step 4: the default is created once, so every call that leaves out the list shares it. Asha rejects the suggestion, and her final program still matches the target.

after.heading: Mistake 1: a local name used outside

after.say: The fix: return message, and store the returned value.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: a keyword, then a position

segments.say: Mistake 2 is the quick check from step 5. After a keyword argument, every argument needs a name, so Python cannot even read the file.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the answer appears.

segments.say: One more. Look at the def line, and remember the rule from step 4.

after.say: The parameter with a default, rate, comes before price, which has none. Parameters with a default go last.
after.heading: Mistake 3: a default too early

after.say: The fix: price first, then rate equals 1.1.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: a list as a default

segments.say: Mistake 4 is the AI's suggestion again, with no error. Lina and Omar share one order. The fix: no default list; pass a new empty list in each call.

items: Return what you need outside.
Defaults last, keywords last.
Never a list as a default.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then a final quick check, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A local variable lives inside its function, only while it runs.
A function can read a global, but then its result depends on a hidden line.
Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local for the whole function.
Pass values in, return results out. A pure function does only that.
Defaults make a parameter optional. Keywords name it in the call. Never a list as a default.
Save the output before an AI change, and compare after every change.

segments.say: Let's recap. A local variable lives inside its function. A function can read a global, but its result then depends on a hidden line.
Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local for the whole function. So pass values in, and return results out.
Defaults make a parameter optional, keywords name it, and a list is never a default. And with AI: save the output, and compare after every change.

visual.question: `with_tax(price, rate=1.1)` multiplies the price by the rate. What does `with_tax(10.0, rate=1.2)` return?
visual.explain: The keyword argument replaces the default: 10.0 times 1.2 is 12.0.

segments.say: One last check. With tax is called with 10.0, and rate equals 1.2. What does it return?

after.say: B. 12.0. The keyword argument replaces the default rate.
